extraction.name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
extraction.description: A review paper that critically examines the current state of visual question answering (VQA) in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms, with emphasis on dataset limitations, biases, and future directions.
extraction.creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan
extraction.citeAs: Kafle, K. and Kanan, C. Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges. arXiv:1610.01465v4, 2017.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: This paper is a review and does not introduce a new dataset. It describes data collection procedures used by existing VQA datasets. Examples explicitly discussed include: COCO-QA, where QA pairs are created for images using an NLP algorithm derived from COCO image captions; COCO-VQA, where Amazon Mechanical Turk workers generated questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers generated answers; Visual Genome, which used two distinct modes of data collection, a free-form method where annotators were free to ask any question about an image and a region-specific method where workers were prompted to ask questions about specific image regions using descriptive bounding-box annotations; Visual7W, a subset of Visual Genome, using multiple-choice answers with plausible distractors collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image; FM-IQA, containing human generated questions and answers originally collected in Chinese; and SHAPES, consisting of synthetic shape images with systematically generated binary questions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Experiments
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The reviewed datasets draw from images from NYU-DepthV2, Microsoft COCO, Flickr100M/YFCC100M, synthetic cartoon scenes, and synthetic shape images. COCO-QA derives QA pairs from COCO image captions using an NLP algorithm. Visual Genome uses COCO and YFCC100M images plus descriptive bounding-box annotations. Visual7W is a subset of Visual Genome using images also present in COCO.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The paper describes several dataset-specific manipulations: COCO-QA automatically derives question-answer pairs from captions using an NLP algorithm, including breaking longer sentences into smaller chunks; The VQA Dataset includes an open-ended format and a multiple-choice format where choices are composed of the correct answer, plausible answers, popular answers, and random answers; Visual7W uses multiple-choice answers with plausible distractors; SHAPES systematically asks every question about each image, making it completely balanced.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing by the NLP algorithm that generates QA pairs from captions. For The VQA Dataset, the multiple-choice format is constructed from the same QA pairs by adding 18 answer choices from several sources. For FDA on COCO annotations during testing, object labels are obtained by classifying bounding boxes using ResNet, but this is part of algorithm evaluation rather than dataset preprocessing.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper describes annotation protocols for existing datasets. In COCO-VQA, Amazon Mechanical Turk workers generated three questions per image by trying to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers generated answers; each question was answered by 10 independent annotators. In DAQUAR-consensus, additional ground truth answers were collected, averaging five human annotated answers per question. In Visual Genome, annotators asked either free-form questions or region-specific questions prompted by image regions with descriptive bounding boxes. In Visual7W, plausible multiple-choice answers were collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image. FM-IQA contains human generated questions and answers and allows full-sentence answers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper discusses consensus-based evaluation and annotator disagreement. For The VQA Dataset, ten answers per question are used with a consensus metric where full credit is given if an algorithm agrees with three or more annotators. The paper notes substantial disagreement, including only 83.3% inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA, poor agreement for 'Why' questions, cases where annotators provide antonyms such as 'left' and 'right,' and cases where both 'yes' and 'no' appear often enough to both receive high scores. DAQUAR-consensus uses average consensus and min consensus based on multiple human answers.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question; DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question; Visual Genome: average of 17 QA pairs per image; COCO-VQA and SYNTH-VQA: 3 questions per image/scene
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: For SYNTH-VQA, the synthetic human cartoon models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance. No demographics of human annotators are provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm for deriving COCO-QA question-answer pairs from captions
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper notes that SYNTH-VQA human cartoon models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that the most immediate application of VQA is as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images both on the web and in the real world. It also notes broader use for improving human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content and for image retrieval without metadata or tags.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper extensively discusses biases in VQA datasets. It states that many datasets contain exploitable biases in question and answer distributions, allowing algorithms to perform well without truly solving VQA. COCO-VQA contains strong language biases, with simple image-blind algorithms achieving 49.6% accuracy using the question alone. Yes/no answers span about 38% of all questions and almost 59% of them are answered with 'yes.' The paper reports that answering 'yes' to all yes/no questions yields 71% under the dataset's evaluation metric. It also notes that human annotators tend to ask similar holistic questions, that natural image datasets have contextual biases, and that synthetic datasets such as SHAPES and Yin and Yang can reduce such biases.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper identifies many limitations of existing VQA datasets. DAQUAR is too small, contains exclusively indoor scenes, and has clutter and extreme lighting conditions. COCO-QA suffers from flaws in the NLP algorithm, producing awkward, grammatically incorrect, or unintelligible questions and only four kinds of questions. COCO-VQA contains many questions answerable without the image due to language biases, subjective opinion-seeking questions without a single objective answer, explanatory or verbose answers that are difficult to evaluate, and only about 83% inter-human agreement. FM-IQA allows full-sentence answers, making automatic evaluation intractable and requiring impractical human judging. Visual Genome and Visual7W have high answer diversity and many multi-word answers, making open-ended evaluation challenging. The paper concludes that existing VQA benchmarks are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has solved VQA.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The datasets reviewed are used to train and evaluate visual question answering systems. The paper discusses both training and evaluation use, including open-ended and multiple-choice benchmarking. It recommends that future datasets be larger, less biased, and evaluated with more nuanced per-question-type analysis rather than naive overall accuracy. It also argues that multiple-choice evaluation alone is insufficient because it can reduce the task to selecting among provided answers rather than actually answering questions.
